groups.title: JWT auth security: token structure and storage
groups.question: Your MEAN app uses JWTs, and a teammate wants to put the user's role and email in the token and store it in localStorage. Explain what is inside a JWT and where it should be stored.

followUps.JWT header.payload.signature: what each: What do the three parts of a JWT contain, and can users read the payload?
followUps.Token storage: why memory > localStorage: What are the trade-offs between memory, localStorage and HttpOnly cookies for a token?

evidence.text: A JWT has a header with the algorithm, a payload with claims and a signature.
The signature proves the token was not changed, using the server's secret.
The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it and it must not hold secrets.

misconceptions.text: Says the JWT payload is encrypted.

evidence.text: Keeping the token in memory is safest from XSS but it is lost on page refresh.
localStorage survives refreshes but any script, including injected ones, can read it.
HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by scripts but need CSRF protection.

groups.title: Angular route guards for client-side protection
groups.question: Signed-out users can open the /tasks page in your Angular app, and a teammate says a route guard makes the API secure. Explain what guards do and what they do not do.

followUps.CanActivate guard: redirecting unauthent: How does a CanActivate guard redirect a signed-out user?
followUps.CanActivate is client-side only — server: Why isn't a route guard enough to protect your data?

evidence.text: The guard checks the auth state before navigation.
It returns true to allow navigation.
Otherwise it returns a URL tree that redirects to the login page.
Guards run in the browser, so anyone can bypass them or call the API directly.
Every API endpoint must verify the token itself.
Guards improve the user experience; security comes from the server.

notEnough: Only saying the server must check too.

misconceptions.text: Says Angular route guards stop unauthorized users from getting data.

groups.title: Implementing JWT auth on the Express backend
groups.question: You are writing the login endpoint and the auth middleware for your Express API. Explain how tokens are created and checked on each request.

followUps.Signing and verifying JWTs with jsonwebt: What does jwt.sign create and why give access tokens a short expiry?
followUps.Auth middleware: extract Bearer token an: What does the auth middleware do with the Authorization header?

evidence.text: jwt.sign creates a token from a payload, a secret and an expiry.
jwt.verify checks the signature and expiry and returns the payload.
A short expiry limits how long a stolen token is useful.
It reads the bearer token from the Authorization header.
It verifies the token and attaches the user to the request.
If verification fails, it returns an unauthorized error through the error middleware.

notEnough: Only saying it checks the token.

groups.title: Angular auth service and HTTP interceptor
groups.question: On the Angular side, the navbar must update instantly on login and logout, and every API call needs the token. Explain how you would build the auth service and interceptor.

followUps.Auth service: storing token, exposing cu: How would an auth service let the whole app react to login and logout?
followUps.JWT interceptor: injecting the Authoriza: How does the interceptor attach the token?

evidence.text: The service keeps the token or user in a BehaviorSubject.
It exposes Observables like isAuthenticated derived from that state.
Sign out clears the state and navigates to login, and every subscriber updates.

notEnough: Only saying the service stores the token.

evidence.text: The interceptor reads the current token from the auth service.
It clones the request with the Authorization header set.
Requests without a token, or to other domains, are passed through unchanged.

notEnough: Only saying it adds a header.
